Senate Rejects War Powers Resolution to Limit Trump’s Attacks on Iran
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
The Senate rejected a war powers resolution on Thursday that would have directed President Trump to seek congressional approval before resuming attacks on Iran. The resolution failed on a vote of 51-48. Three Republicans voted in favor, while Pennsylvania Democratic Senator John Fetterman voted in opposition. The House approved the resolution in September. Both the House and Senate previously approved a war powers resolution back in June, but President Trump largely ignored it. Thursday’s failed vote in the Senate came after Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested he would not block funding for attacks on Iran in the government funding package due by December 11. Meanwhile, a Pentagon official said Thursday the cost of the war on Iran has topped $48 billion. That figure does not include damage to U.S. bases, the cost of providing healthcare to hundreds of injured troops or the tens of billions of dollars in higher fuel costs triggered by the war.

Senate Passes Permitting Reform Bill with Support of 14 Democrats, Including Leader Chuck Schumer
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
The Senate has approved a permitting reform bill that would weaken environmental laws to speed approval of new housing, roads, energy projects and other infrastructure. While the bill would make it easier to build new transmission lines and wind and solar farms, it would also speed construction of fossil fuel power plants and new data centers, including on public lands. Meanwhile, Native leaders and advocacy groups strongly opposed the legislation, saying it would weaken tribal sovereignty and threaten cultural and sacred sites. This is Oregon Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley, who voted “no.”
Sen. Jeff Merkley: “First, it makes it a lot easier to build data centers. Did anybody notice data centers were a big issue in this most recent election? Here we come right in after the election, and we’re going to pass a bill that makes it easier to do data centers by striking down tools that states have when they decide they do not want to have a data center because it threatens key clean air or clean water issues.”
Despite those objections, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, passed on a vote of 62-33 with 14 Democrats in favor, including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer. In a statement, Food & Water Watch said, “Sen. Schumer’s alignment with Republicans over a majority of his own Democratic caucus in voting to advance this terrible pro-polluter, pro-data center permitting bill is all the reason needed to demand that Schumer step down as leader of the Senate Democrats.” The bill now goes to the House and is expected to be voted on the week after next.

Climate Activists Condemn “Slimmed-Down” COP31 Draft Text That Makes No Reference to Fossil Fuels
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
Here at the COP31 U.N. climate summit, negotiators published a “slimmed-down” draft text on Thursday that stripped out any reference to fossil fuels, or ending their use. Instead, the document promotes carbon capture and storage, an unproven technology that critics say will never have a meaningful impact on the climate crisis. Activists at the COP are demanding more financing to help poorer countries adapt to a warming world. This is Iona Stewart of the climate action group Global Witness.
Emily Iona Stewart: “Mentions of human rights, especially human rights and environment defenders, which had previously been introduced by the Brazilians, are now being walked back in this cover decision. So that’s really worrying for us. Another thing: fossil fuels, still not in there. Where is the text on phasing out fossil fuels and having a concrete roadmap for all of the parties? We need that now. And then, finance. There’s not enough momentum on making sure that countries who have already signed up and pledged to give climate finance actually deliver on those pledges.”

Russian Attacks Kill 8 After Ukraine Bombs Bridge Connecting Russia to Occupied Crimea
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
In Ukraine, officials say eight people were killed and dozens injured overnight, as Russia launched a massive drone and missile attack. In Kyiv, Russian bombs struck three ⁠bridges over the Dnipro River. Meanwhile, in Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people.
The Russian attacks came after Ukraine bombed the Kerch Bridge, the only link between mainland Russia and Russian-annexed Crimea. Engineers say it could take years for Russia to repair the damage.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the bridge strike and warned of further action.
President Volodymyr Zelensky: “We have long been telling Russia: Enough of striking bridges, our cities and villages, Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, railways and grain ships. Enough of this war. But every time, Russia chooses a new escalation.”
Meanwhile, Poland’s military said it was investigating a suspected violation of its airspace by Russia near Poland’s border with Ukraine, after an unidentified object crash-landed this morning.

Charity Warns Record High 1 in 4 Children Now Live in Conflict Zones
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
A new report by Save the Children has found one in four children now live in conflict zones worldwide — a record high. In Africa, an unprecedented two in five children are impacted by conflict. Almost one-third of all violations against children documented last year took place in the Occupied Palestinian Territories, where Israeli attacks have killed at least 22,000 children since 2023.

11-Year-Old Palestinian Boy Dies of Wounds Amid Relentless Israeli Attacks on Gaza
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
In Gaza, 11-year-old Mansour Khader Nabhan has died of his wounds after he was bombed by an Israeli quadcopter in Jabaliya. In a separate strike, several children were wounded when an Israeli drone targeted a group of Palestinians, including some on their way to school. On Thursday, Israeli attacks left at least five Palestinians dead, including two people killed by a drone near a community kitchen serving displaced people in Gaza City.

Somali American Driver Is Assaulted After Trump Calls on Minnesotans to “Fight Back” Against Somalis
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
In Minnesota, a Somali American Uber driver is fighting for his life after he was allegedly run over multiple times with his own vehicle by a passenger who disliked his Muslim name. Mohamed Yusuf remained in critical condition Thursday with life-threatening injuries following Saturday’s attack. It follows last month’s raid on the D.C. home of Somali American Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar by federal agents. And it follows president Trump’s repeated racist attacks demonizing Somali American communities. Trump has called Somalis “garbage” and “low-IQ people” who “contribute nothing.” Just weeks ago, Trump wrote on social media, “Fight back Minnesota, fight back!”

“A Mockery of Court Orders”: Federal Judge Holds ICE in Contempt for Rearresting Immigrants
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
A Colorado federal judge has held ICE officials and the Trump administration in contempt over a practice to instantly rearrest immigrants after a court has ordered their release from ICE jail. In her ruling, U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney wrote that ICE “made ⁠a mockery of court orders.” The ACLU has described the practice as “sham releases.” At the center of the case is the detention of Mexican immigrant Ramón Quintero Álvarez, who has lived in the U.S. for more than 30 years. Álvarez was immediately rearrested late last month shortly after his release from an Aurora ICE jail.

U.S. Appeals Court Freezes Deportation Protections for Venezuelan Immigrants
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
A federal appeals court is allowing the Trump administration to end, for now, deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan immigrants living in the U.S. This came as the Trump administration also filed an emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court in its effort to end temporary protected status for an estimated 600,000 Venezuelans. Since returning to office, Trump has ended the humanitarian relief for well over a dozen countries as part of his mass deportation campaign.

Texas Death Row Prisoner Reinaldo Dennes Cries Out in Pain During Botched Execution
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
In Huntsville, Texas, a man on death row repeatedly moaned out in pain during a botched execution that took over an hour. Reinaldo Dennes remained strapped to a gurney as prison officials struggled to locate a vein to administer a lethal dose of pentobarbital. After more than an hour Thursday evening, vein lines were ultimately found in his neck and one of his feet. Seventy-year-old Dennes reportedly exclaimed that his leg felt like it was on fire. This comes just over a month after the botched execution attempt of Christa Pike in Tennessee that drew widespread condemnation. Pike survived two lethal injections and was left hospitalized in critical condition and unconscious for nearly a week. She’s now back in prison.
Topics:
Death Penalty

Florida Carries Out 20th Execution This Year, a Record Pace
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
Florida carried out a 20th execution this year, breaking its own record as the highest single-year total of executions in Florida since capital punishment was reinstated in 1976. Seventy-one-year-old Thomas Mitchell Overton was put to death by lethal injection Thursday. Florida has now carried out more than half of the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Governor Ron DeSantis. Two more are scheduled for December.

Death Penalty
Florida
White House Taps GOP Operative and Lobbyist Eric Ueland to Lead Government Accountability Office
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
The White House has picked Eric Ueland to run the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s independent watchdog, for a 15-year term. Ueland is a longtime Republican operative who served as a Big Pharma and fossil fuel lobbyist before joining the Trump administration in 2016. Senate Republicans are skipping the bipartisan process used for every GAO head since 1980, in which top lawmakers submit a short list of candidates. Twenty-one inspectors general are urging congressional leaders to reject Ueland’s confirmation, writing, “the credibility of any oversight institution depends on two pillars: strict adherence to statutory safeguards designed to protect its independence, and leadership defined by proven, nonpartisan fidelity to objective evidence. Mr. Ueland’s nomination fails on both counts.”
Topics:
Congress
Republican Party
Donald Trump
Journalist Camilo Rodríquez, Who Exposed Costa Rican Politicians’ Drug Trafficking Ties, Is Murdered
Nov 20, 2026
Link copied
In Costa Rica, journalist Camilo Rodríguez has been assassinated. Rodríguez gained prominence for exposing alleged links between suspected drug traffickers and Costa Rican politicians. He was reportedly ambushed and gunned down while driving in heavy traffic on a highway outside of the capital San José Monday. The Committee to Protect Journalists is demanding an investigation. Rodríguez had previously reported threats to his life. This is the first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years.

Latin America

El Senado de EE.UU. rechaza una resolución de poderes de guerra para limitar los ataques de Trump contra Irán
20 Nov. 2026
Link copied
El Senado de Estados Unidos rechazó el jueves una resolución de poderes de guerra que habría obligado al presidente Trump a obtener la aprobación del Congreso antes de reanudar los ataques contra Irán. La resolución obtuvo 48 votos a favor y 51 en contra. Tres republicanos votaron a favor de la medida, mientras que el senador demócrata del estado de Pensilvania John Fetterman votó en contra. La Cámara de Representantes había aprobado la resolución en septiembre. Tanto la Cámara de Representantes como el Senado estadounidenses habían aprobado en junio pasado una resolución de poderes de guerra sobre Irán, pero Trump la ignoró en gran medida. La votación del jueves en el Senado en contra de la resolución se produjo después de que el líder del bloque demócrata en la Cámara de Representantes, Hakeem Jeffries, sugiriera que no iba a bloquear la asignación de fondos para los ataques contra Irán en el paquete de gastos públicos que debe aprobarse antes del 11 de diciembre. Mientras tanto, un funcionario del Pentágono afirmó el jueves que el costo de la guerra contra Irán ha superado los 48.000 millones de dólares. Esa cifra no incluye los daños a bases estadounidenses, los gastos de atención sanitaria de cientos de soldados heridos, ni el sobrecosto de decenas de miles de millones de dólares en combustible generado por la guerra.

El Senado de EE.UU. aprueba una legislación de reforma de permisos de construcción con el apoyo de 14 demócratas, incluido el líder del bloque demócrata, Chuck Schumer
20 Nov. 2026
Link copied
El Senado de Estados Unidos ha aprobado un proyecto de ley de reforma del sistema de permisos de construcción que debilitaría las leyes de protección ambiental con el fin de acelerar la autorización de proyectos inmobiliarios, viales, energéticos y de otras obras de infraestructura. Aunque el proyecto de ley simplificaría los trámites para construir nuevas líneas de transmisión y parques de energía eólica y solar, también aceleraría el desarrollo de centrales de generación eléctrica a partir de combustibles fósiles y de nuevos centros de datos, incluso en tierras de propiedad pública. Mientras tanto, líderes indígenas y organizaciones activistas se opusieron enérgicamente a la nueva legislación, al considerar que esta menoscabaría la soberanía de pueblos originarios y amenazaría sitios sagrados y de importancia cultural. Estas fueron las palabras expresadas por el senador demócrata del estado de Oregón Jeff Merkley, quien votó en contra del proyecto de ley.
Senador Jeff Merkley: “En primer lugar, [esta legislación] hace que sea mucho más fácil construir centros de datos. ¿Alguien notó que los centros de datos fueron un tema importante en estas últimas elecciones? Y ahora, justo después de los comicios, vamos a aprobar un proyecto de ley que facilita la construcción de centros de datos al eliminar las herramientas de las que disponen los estados para impedir su instalación cuando consideran que representan una amenaza para cuestiones fundamentales como la calidad del aire o del agua potable”.
A pesar de estas objeciones, la Ley Bipartidista de Asequibilidad y Empleo en Estados Unidos (conocida como BAAJA, por sus siglas en inglés) fue aprobada por 62 votos contra 33 y contó con el respaldo de 14 demócratas, entre ellos el líder del bloque demócrata del Senado, Chuck Schumer. La organización Food & Water Watch afirmó en un comunicado: “El hecho de que el senador Schumer se haya alineado con los republicanos —en contra de la mayoría de su propio bloque demócrata— para impulsar este nefasto proyecto de ley a favor de los contaminadores y los centros de datos es motivo más que suficiente para exigir que renuncie a su cargo como líder de los demócratas en el Senado”. El proyecto de ley pasará ahora a consideración de la Cámara de Representantes, donde se prevé que sea sometido a votación dentro de dos semanas.

Activistas ambientales critican el borrador “recortado” del documento final de la COP31 que no hace referencia a los combustibles fósiles
20 Nov. 2026
Link copied
En la Conferencia de las Naciones Unidas sobre el Cambio Climático, conocida como COP31, los negociadores publicaron el jueves un borrador “recortado” del documento final que elimina toda referencia a los combustibles fósiles o a la necesidad de poner fin a su uso. En cambio, el documento promueve la captura y el almacenamiento de carbono, una tecnología cuya efectividad no ha sido comprobada y que, según los críticos, nunca tendrá un impacto significativo en la crisis climática. Activistas presentes en la conferencia climática de la ONU están exigiendo más financiación para ayudar a los países más pobres a adaptarse al aumento de la temperatura global. Estas fueron las palabras expresadas por Iona Stewart, de la organización de acción climática Global Witness.
Emily Iona Stewart: “Las referencias a los derechos humanos, especialmente a los defensores de los derechos humanos y del medioambiente, que la delegación brasileña había incorporado anteriormente, ahora están siendo eliminadas de esta decisión marco. Eso nos preocupa mucho. The world’s top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country’s Rohingya Muslim minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 refugees into Bangladesh. The landmark ruling is the first time the International Court of Justice has held a nation directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. “This is a vindication of what Rohingyas have been saying for the last almost 50 years, since 1978, when the first wave of genocidal expulsion was conducted by the very same perpetrating institution,” says Burmese dissident scholar Maung Zarni. By recognizing Myanmar’s “identity-based group destruction” of the Royinghas, he says, “the court vindicated [the] Rohingya’s collective articulation, memory and suffering.”
“For the first time in its history, the court has set up a process for restitution and reparation for the members of the Rohingya community,” explains Philippe Sands, an international human rights lawyer who served on the legal team for The Gambia, which first brought the legal case against Myanmar to the ICJ six years ago. Sands discusses next steps for restitution and reparations to Rohingya victims, as well as what the Myanmar judgment means for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, also before the ICJ.

AMY GOODMAN: Later in the broadcast, we’ll speak with three leading environmental justice advocates, from Malaysia, from Ethiopia and from India. But right now we go to this top story out of The Hague. This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.
In a historic decision, the International Court of Justice in The Hague has ruled Myanmar, also known as Burma, committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims during a 2017 military crackdown that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. It’s the first time the court has held a nation directly responsible for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. The presiding judge of the International Court, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, read the ruling.
JUDGE YUJI IWASAWA: For these reasons, the court, one, by nine votes to six, finds that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. … The court has also determined that the estimate of 10,000 Rohingya violently killed during those clearance operations is supported by the evidence. … On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.
AMY GOODMAN: The genocide case against Burma, or Myanmar, was brought by The Gambia, the smallest country in mainland Africa. Gambia’s Justice Minister Dawda Jallow spoke in The Hague after the ruling.
DAWDA JALLOW: Today, the International Court of Justice confirmed what Rohingya have said since 2017: What was done to them was genocide, and Myanmar is responsible. The court has found that Myanmar breached the 1948 convention, Genocide Convention, and has ordered to make reparations. This is the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide, the crime of crimes. The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived, they testified, and today they were believed.

In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change.
“This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on Democracy Now! by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries.
“At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, [are] saying is, 'There is no money at home.' But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”

Climate advocacy groups and Indigenous organizations from across the world have slammed this gathering as the “worst COP ever” and rejected the latest draft text as a “disaster,” urging developing countries to reject the latest draft text.
Meanwhile, at a news conference just before our broadcast, Panama’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro has threatened to block any final agreement if it doesn’t include a cap on oil production. Earlier this week, he spoke out forcefully against the role of what he described as the “petroleum mafia.”

The first is that science must be the foundation. Everything we do must be based on science.
Second, we need a clear transition away from fossil fuels. It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. AMY GOODMAN: We now turn to a little girl, 8-year-old Marren Akeyo of Kenya, holds the title Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026.
MARREN AKEYO: Good morning, COP31. Good morning, Your Excellencies, distinguished guests, professors, teachers, parents and all the very important people here today.
My name is Marren Akeyo. I am 8 years old. Yes, only 8. I know some of you are wondering what this small girl is doing at COP31. Yes, I might be small, but my dreams are taller than some of the trees you have planted.
I am Little Miss Environment Kenya, overall Mini Miss Kenya, a model, a climate champion and the founder of Akeyo Foundation. But please, don’t be confused by my crown. I am not the queen of sitting pretty; I am the queen of getting my hands dirty.
My farm, my classroom. Near my home is a wonderful place called Impact SMART Solution demo farm. That is where I teach children how to plant food and take care of our planet. Some children love playing with their phones. Me, I love playing with soil. And guess what: My vegetables don’t need Wi-Fi; they need water, sunshine, good soil and a little love. At the farm, I learn how to grow food and take care of our planet.
And also, why I started Akeyo Foundation, ladies and gentlemen, I have discovered something very important. You don’t need to be big to solve big problems. That is why I started Akeyo Foundation. My dream is to help children discover their talents, learn smart farming, protect nature and become environmental champions.
I invite my friends to the farm so that we can learn and plan together, because when I teach one child and that child teaches another child, soon we’ll have a whole generation of climate champions.
And let me tell you something: Climate change does not ask for your birth certificate before affecting you. So, why should we wait until we’re adults to protect our planet? We children are ready to plant.
My crown has a job. I also love modeling, dancing, singing, poetry, swimming, skating and cycling. Yes, I have many talents. Sometimes I even think my talents need a timetable. But my biggest dream is not to collect crown and trophies. My biggest dream is making my talents useful to the world, because a crown on my head is beautiful, but a tree growing because of my hand is much more beautiful.
My challenge to the world, now I have a question for all the big people here today. You have big offices, big cars, big meetings, and sometimes very big speeches. But tell me: How big is your action for our planet? We children are ready to plant. We are ready to grow food. We are ready to take care of our planet. But we need you to give us opportunities. Don’t just tell us, “You’re the leaders of tomorrow.” Let us lead something today. Start with what you have.
Now I need your help. When I say “COP,” you say “31.” COP!
AUDIENCE: Thirty-one!
MARREN AKEYO: COP!
AUDIENCE: Thirty-one!
MARREN AKEYO: When I say “little hands,” you say “big change.” Little hands!
AUDIENCE: Big change!
MARREN AKEYO: Little hands!
AUDIENCE: Big change!
MARREN AKEYO: And finally, I am Marren Akeyo. I am only 8 years old. I may be not old enough to drive a car, but I am old enough to drive change.
Thank you, COP31. Let us make our planet green again. I am representing the voice of children, not to just speak for — not to just speak for phones, not to just speak for electronics, but I am speaking for our environment and climate. Thank you.
AMY GOODMAN: So, that’s Marren Akeyo, 8-year-old Kenyan activist, holds the title of Little Miss Environment Kenya 2026. She spoke at COP31, the climate summit, on Thursday.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: We turn now to The Book of Genocides, an illustrated graphic narrative that tells the story of 10 genocides across five centuries, from the First Peoples of the Americas, the transatlantic slave trade, the Armenian genocide, the Holocaust, Palestine and beyond. In the tradition of Art Spiegelman and Joe Sacco, Dana Mashoian Walrath uses comics to tell harrowing stories from history.
AMY GOODMAN: Dana Mashoian Walrath is an award-winning artist and anthropologist. Her own grandmother survived the Armenian genocide as a child by hiding in an urn.
Welcome to Democracy Now!, Dana. This is an incredible book, The Book of Genocides. Talk about why you decided to write it, to illustrate it, this incredible graphic novel.
DANA WALRATH: Well, first, thank you for having me here. It’s an honor.
I wanted to write it to end the violence. We’ve got violence surrounding us, not just bombs dropping all over the world, but the systemic and structural violence that is selectively hurting some people and helping others. And I wanted to put it into comics form because it’s immediately accessible in ways that academic papers and even prose isn’t quite as accessible, because with comics, we see it. It’s there in our hands. And it’s sort of like a film or a play that you can turn the pages, and you can get involved with what’s happening there.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And let’s begin with this, the story of your grandmother who survived the Armenian genocide as a child by hiding in an urn. If you could tell us when you learned about that story and how it kind of shaped your interests, and then this eventually resulting in this book?
DANA WALRATH: Thank you. That story only came to me about five years ago. I was calling my mother’s older sister. And I had already written a verse novel about the Armenian genocide. And once I had done that, all of a sudden the older generation started sharing stories with me. And my aunt told me that my grandmother hid inside the urn while her father was being dismembered, and that her mother and younger brother were taken into enslavement.
AMY GOODMAN: Wait. Explain. That was way too fast. Hid in what kind of urn? While?
DANA WALRATH: Yeah, I’m sure her parents helped her get inside there, or her mother. In Armenian culture, they have these giant ceramic urns. And so, on the first page of the book, you could see one of them. So, they would store grain. My family, my grandmother’s family, they were millers, so they had urns filled with grain. But there would be urns filled with wine that would be fermenting. So, it’s really one of our traditional cultural pieces of equipment. And they had an empty one, and the genocide was starting to come to where they were. And —
AMY GOODMAN: When you say the genocide was starting, explain the Armenian genocide.
DANA WALRATH: OK. The Armenian genocide, it was at its height in 1915. Armenians were colonized by the Ottomans starting at the end of the 12th century, and then going through — I should have said 13th. Sorry. The Ottomans colonized the Armenians when they swept in from Central Asia, and all the other people throughout lots of Europe, across North Africa and so forth.
And when the Ottoman Empire was dissolving, the Armenians, who were already second-class citizens, paid higher taxes, were kept out of military service and so forth, just the way we see apartheid today, say, in Gaza and the West Bank, and the way we saw apartheid in South Africa before. It was an apartheid against Jewish and Christian citizens, and actually even against Shia Muslims. It was a preference for Sunni Muslims, who had all the power.
And when the empire was collapsing as countries found their own independence, the Ottomans began a systematic blaming of their minorities and developed an ideology of pan-Turkism to make a continuous republic going from today’s Turkey into the Central Asian Turkic republics that we know today

Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted his U.S. and Russian counterparts for a historic trilateral summit on Thursday, with the leaders of the three biggest nuclear superpowers meeting for about 90 minutes in Shenzhen. Afterward, the countries published a “peace declaration” that affirmed “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” The declaration also announced a commitment to increase petroleum production, called for reforms at the United Nations and urged the International Criminal Court and similar bodies to “not abuse their jurisdiction.”
While in China, President Donald Trump also had a separate meeting with President Vladimir Putin to discuss the war in Ukraine, though it’s unclear if they made any progress.
“It’s a significant post-1945 moment, which was the last time that we had great summits,” says Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin. “What is the most important takeaway … is an ascendant China. It was China that really set the terms of what was said.”

NERMEEN SHAIKH: We begin today’s show looking at today’s historic trilateral summit in China between Chinese President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The three leaders met for about 90 minutes.
After the meeting, Chinese state media issued what it described as a, quote, “peace declaration” by the Chinese, Russian and U.S. leaders. The four-point declaration called for reforms at the United Nations and said the three leaders, quote, “concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.” The three countries are not signatories to the ICC. The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes committed in Ukraine.
The declaration also states, quote, “The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.”
In addition, the declaration states, quote, “The three countries will engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation.”
AMY GOODMAN: Prior to the closed-door meeting, the three leaders shared brief remarks. This is Chinese President Xi Jinping.
PRESIDENT XI JINPING: [translated] This is the first time the leaders of our three countries have come together. It is a historic meeting. We will discuss how to safeguard world peace and promote strategic stability and relations among major powers. …
The world is undergoing rapid changes unseen in a century. The world is not peaceful, and challenges reveal true leadership. As major world powers and permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, our three nations should lead by example, collaborate to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability, and make more significant contributions to the progress of humanity.
AMY GOODMAN: Russian President Vladimir Putin also spoke before the trilateral meeting in China.
PRESIDENT VLADIMIR PUTIN: [translated] For my part, I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, and our respective peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening global security and stability, provided they engage in constructive, partnership-based cooperation rooted in mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And this is President Trump speaking in China before the trilateral meeting.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: As presidents of three of the world’s largest countries, we have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet. Too often past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite, and we think that we are sure about that. No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them, so no peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech.
AMY GOODMAN: Well, we’re joined right now by Scott Lucas. He’s a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute.
